newsitem.title: USA: Talks with armed separatists in Texas break down.
newsitem.headline: Talks with armed separatists in Texas break down.

text.p: Communications with an armed separatist group holed up in a mountain compound in Texas have broken down with no agreement to end a four-day-old standoff with police, authorities said on Wednesday.
They said the Republic of Texas group had halted telephone negotiations with police for unknown reasons after negotiators came close to a deal with separatist leader Richard McLaren.
"There was the optimistic feeling they were going to sign an agreement. The agreement has never been signed," Texas Department of Public Safety spokesman Mike Cox told reporters.
"We thought we had open dialgoue with him and then, kerplunk, the wheel fell off," Cox said. Negotiators have been sending faxes to the group asking them to call to no avail.
Despite the setback in talks, Cox said police were in no hurry to move in. "We have no time table, we are not contemplating any assault...we are handling this peacefully."

The Republic of Texas, which was formed in 1995, advocates the secession of Texas from the United States. It claims to have thousands of members and links to anti-goverment militia groups around the country.

The standoff began on Sunday when group members took two hostages in retaliation for the arrest of their security chief, Robert Scheidt. The hostages were later released in exchange for Scheidt, but felony criminal charges with penalties of up to 99 years in prison have been filed against six of the separatists, including McLaren.

Since Sunday, an estimated 120 police have poured into the Davis Mountains in west Texas to surround the remote compound. Their arsenal includes two armoured personnel carriers. On Wednesday, a trailer was brought in carrying four horses and nine bloodhounds used to search for escaped convicts.
Earlier, police detained seven men in Pecos, Texas on the suspicion they were going to join the separatist group. Fully automatic weapons were found in two cars belonging to the men.

On Tuesday, authorities issued a warning that three men from a California-based militia may be headed to Fort Davis to help the Republic of Texas group, but it was not clear if the men detained in Pecos were the same suspects.
Cox urged any Republic of Texas sympathisers thinking of joining the siege to stay away.
"This is not the Alamo, this is not San Jacinto, I'm not Davy Crockett," he said, referring to the sites of famous battles and fighters in Texas' 1836 war for independence from Mexico.
